The real scandal? SNAP’s $30B Thrifty Food Plan adjustment freeze in the 2024 Farm Bill proves DC prioritizes bureaucratic bloat over actual hunger relief. While Reps clutch pearls over “cuts,” they ignore how SNAP’s own structure funnels cash into admin costs and failed privatization schemes—like the 2021 Texas outsourcing disaster that delayed benefits for 300k families.

This “anti-hunger” program spends $6.4B annually on overhead while 40% of participants still face food insecurity. Redirecting funds to block grants would let states innovate—like New Hampshire’s 2023 pilot tying benefits to local farm purchases, boosting agriculture 12%.

The choice isn’t between feeding families or fiscal sanity—it’s about ending D.C.’s monopoly on failure.

SNAP’s 14.33% error rate in New Jersey proves systemic waste—overpayments and bureaucratic bloat drain taxpayer dollars. The Big Beautiful Bill forces states to share costs, incentivizing accountability after decades of unchecked federal spending. When 40% of errors stem from recipients’ failure to report income or household changes, it’s not a “war on families”—it’s a demand for basic program integrity.

New Jersey’s $100M-$300M cost-sharing burden? A drop in the bucket compared to the $186B saved nationally by ending blank-check subsidies.

Work requirements for able-bodied adults up to age 64 aren’t cruelty—they’re a return to the program’s original purpose: temporary aid, not generational dependency.

The numbers don’t lie—see how the real costs and savings stack up: https://t.co/0aR8ughnL8

School meals matter, but let’s cut through the spin. The proposed $660M slash to Local Food for Schools (LFS) programs—redirecting funds from fresh, local student meals to foreign aid slush funds—is peak D.C. dysfunction. While bureaucrats cry “cuts,” they’re silent on the 18% admin bloat in USDA’s nutrition division (FY2024 audit).

Real solutions? Redirect every dollar from UN climate grants to American farms, mandate 80% of school food budgets stay in-state, and sunset SNAP’s 12 redundant subprograms.

Protect kids, not pork.
